title: You're worth $700 dead — I wrote to 5 government agencies about it
content: It started with a study. In the US, companies extract an estimated $700 worth of data per user — and that doesn't stop when you die. Your accounts stay active, your data keeps circulating, your digital ghost keeps generating ad revenue. That pissed me off. The rabbit hole: France actually passed a law in 2016 (article 85 of the Loi Informatique et Libertés) giving citizens post-mortem rights over their personal data. The problem? Almost nobody knows it exists, and there's no infrastructure to exercise those rights. Families spend months navigating fragmented processes to close accounts while companies keep profiting from the dead. The proposal: I wrote a formal letter to five French government agencies proposing an extension of France Identité — the national digital identity platform. The idea: a post-mortem digital mandate system. You designate a trusted person as your digital executor, you express your wishes (delete my data, transfer my accounts, nuke everything), and when your death is officially certified, those instructions are automatically dispatched to every service provider via a secure API. France would be the first country to integrate this into a certified national identity system — not leaving it to Google's Inactive Account Manager or Apple's Digital Legacy. Then it grew. Talking about it with my mom, I realized this shouldn't only activate after death. Why not right now? You could link your accounts to your France Identité profile and say: this Gmail account is mine, and I want the right to request full deletion of everything Google has on me with one click. A centralized, government-backed "forget me" button. And then inheritance. When you die, someone inherits your house, your car, your books. But your Kindle library? Your audiobooks? Your Steam games? Most platforms say no — you bought a license, not ownership, and it dies with you. That's absurd. Steam has Family Sharing — you can lend your library to relatives while you're alive. But when you die? Your account is non-transferable, cannot be passed on via a will, and your entire library dies with you. They solved sharing but not inheritance. This should be illegal. The bigger picture: Data deletion after death, right-to-erasure enforcement while alive, and digital inheritance of purchased goods — these are three faces of the same problem. We don't have digital sovereignty. Companies treat our data as their property and our purchases as temporary permissions. If France or the EU steps up to enforce all three, it changes the relationship between citizens and platforms fundamentally. I contacted five agencies. Now I wait.

title: Slay the Spire 2 broke my brain — now I'm building a cyberpunk deck-builder
content: Slay the Spire 2 dropped and I lost a weekend to it. Then I lost another weekend thinking "I could build something like this." That itch — the same one that led to PokeBattleTower — came back hard. Except this time I wanted to go darker. Cyberpunk. Netrunners. Heat mechanics instead of mana. Day one: I scaffolded with Vite + React 19 + TypeScript + Zustand and immediately made a decision I'm proud of — no game framework. No Phaser, no PixiJS. Pure React for UI, raw Canvas for the map, and a clean separation: game/ holds pure logic with zero React imports, components/ is UI, stores/ bridges them. This means every game system is testable without rendering anything. The heat system is what makes it mine. Cards generate heat. Safe zone, overclocked, redline, crash — push too hard and your cyberdeck melts. Enemies run on the same system. That symmetry felt right. Where it stands: Title screen with a boot sequence animation, lore crawl with typewriter effect, loadout picker with 3 cyberdecks, canvas-rendered branching map à la StS, and a battle screen that just landed. The game logic layer is typed but empty — combat engine, card effects, enemy AI are all next. I'm genuinely excited to keep going.

title: Building the Laravel Breeze of Symfony — because it should exist
content: Every time I start a Symfony project, I redo the same auth scaffolding. Login, register, email verification, password reset, maybe OAuth. Laravel has Breeze — one command and you're done. Symfony doesn't have an equivalent. So I'm building one. The philosophy: composer require, run php bin/console auth:install, answer two prompts (Google OAuth? Sender email?), and you have a complete auth system. After install, you own all the code — no runtime dependency on my package. It scaffolds User entity, controllers, forms, Twig templates, security config, the whole thing. Then it gets out of your way. The hard part wasn't the auth code itself — it was making the installer smart. It needs to detect your database config, register bundles, scaffold files without clobbering existing ones, and give clear feedback. I spent more time on the InstallCommand than on any controller. Why this matters to me: I want to contribute to open source. Not just use it — put my signature on something. Building tools that save other developers time is the kind of work that makes you grow. It forces you to think about DX, edge cases you'd never hit in your own projects, and what "good defaults" actually means.

title: I built a security scanner in two days — here's what I learned about vulnerabilities
content: Application security is one of those things everyone knows matters and almost nobody does well. Vulnerabilities are rampant — even in popular packages. I wanted to understand the problem space deeply, so I built SecureScan: submit a repo, run multiple scanners concurrently, map everything to OWASP Top 10:2025, and generate actionable fixes. The stack: Go + Fiber v3 for the API (concurrency is a first-class citizen — perfect for orchestrating Semgrep, TruffleHog, npm audit, and ESLint in parallel), SvelteKit for the frontend with SSE for real-time scan progress, PostgreSQL for persistence. Two days, monorepo, zero shortcuts. The fix engine is what I'm most proud of. Template-based generators for the 5 most common vulnerability patterns (SQL injection, XSS, insecure deps, leaked secrets, weak passwords), plus an optional Claude-powered AI fixer for everything else. Accept a fix, and SecureScan branches your repo, applies patches in reverse line order (so line numbers don't shift), commits, pushes, and opens a PR. That reverse-order trick took me an embarrassing amount of time to figure out. What surprised me: The OWASP mapping was harder than the scanning. Tools report findings differently — some give you CWEs, some don't. I ended up building a three-tier fallback: direct metadata match → CWE lookup → heuristic classification. Security isn't just about finding problems — it's about making the findings understandable and fixable.

title: Adding fuzzy search and new sections to VraithUI
content: The portfolio now has a fuzzy matching engine powering both the command palette (Ctrl+K) and console Tab completion. Typing 'tls' finds 'theme list', 'prj' matches 'open projects'. The scoring system has six tiers — exact, starts-with, word-boundary, substring, acronym, and fuzzy subsequence. Three new sections joined the family: skills.rs (Rust-themed with cargo build animation and animated progress bars), blog.sh (git log-style posts), and resume.json (syntax-highlighted JSON with collapsible sections). Key technical choices: The fuzzy engine is a pure function utility with zero dependencies — shared by both UI consumers without coupling. The suggestion dropdown uses absolute positioning with bottom:100% to overlay the scroll area without disrupting the console's flex layout.
